question: What is a module in Python?
correct: A file of Python code that you can import into another file
incorrect: A single function that returns a value to its caller
A blueprint that describes the data an object will hold
A loop that repeats a block of code many times
feedback: A module is a file of Python code. Importing it lets you reuse its functions and values from another file instead of copying code.

question: What is the main benefit of putting reusable code in a module and importing it?
correct: You write the code once and can fix it in a single place
incorrect: Your program runs without needing Python installed
The code becomes impossible for others to read
Every variable in the file turns into a constant
feedback: Modules end copy-paste: write the code once, import it everywhere, and a fix in one file updates every place that uses it.

question: Write the Python statement that imports the standard-library module named math.
correct: import math
feedback: import math makes the math module's functions and values available, accessed as math.something.

question: In the expression  math.pi, what does the  math  part tell you?
correct: That pi lives inside the math namespace
incorrect: That pi is a method you must call with parentheses
That pi is a variable you defined in your own file
That math is the name of your current program
feedback: A namespace answers 'where does this name live?' math.pi means the name pi is found inside the math module's namespace.

question: What is the Python standard library?
correct: A collection of modules that ship with Python and need no install
incorrect: A folder of code files that you wrote yourself
A website where Python programs are published
The single file that holds your main program
feedback: The standard library is the set of modules (math, random, datetime, and many more) that come with Python automatically.

question: Which of the following are true about Python modules and the standard library? (Select all that apply)
correct: A module is a file of Python code you can import
Standard-library modules ship with Python and need no install
Importing lets you reuse code without copying it
incorrect: You must rewrite a module's code in each file that uses it
math and random must be downloaded before you can import them
feedback: Modules are importable files, the standard library comes built in, and importing replaces copy-paste. You neither rewrite nor download standard-library modules.

question: The keyword used to bring code from another module into your file is ___.
correct: import
feedback: import math (or from math import pi) brings names from another module into your file.

question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
correct: A class is a blueprint; an object is a specific thing built from it
incorrect: A class holds data while an object holds only methods
A class is built from many objects stored together
A class runs once while an object runs continuously
feedback: A class describes the data and methods a type will have. An object (or instance) is one concrete thing stamped out from that blueprint, with its own data.

question: What is another word for an object in Python?
correct: An instance
incorrect: A module
A namespace
A parameter
feedback: An instance is one specific thing built from a class. 'Object' and 'instance' mean the same thing.

question: Write the Python header line that begins the definition of a class named Dog. (Just the header, no body.)
correct: class Dog:
feedback: A class definition starts with the keyword class, the name, and a colon: class Dog:

question: What is the role of the  __init__  method in a class?
correct: It sets up a new object automatically when the object is created
incorrect: It deletes an object once the program has finished
It is called by name every time you use the object
It prints the object's data to the screen for the user
feedback: __init__ is the setup method. Python runs it automatically when you create an object, and you never call it by name yourself.

question: The special setup method that runs automatically when an object is created is named ___.
correct: __init__
feedback: __init__ (two underscores on each side) initializes a new object's attributes when it is created.

question: What does  self  refer to inside a method?
correct: The particular object the method was called on
incorrect: The class blueprint rather than any one object
The most recently imported Python module
The value the method is about to return
feedback: self is the current object. Because every method receives self, the same method can act on the data of whichever object it was called on.

question: What is the first parameter of (almost) every method in a class?
correct: self
incorrect: init
class
object
feedback: Methods take self as their first parameter so they can read and change the data of the object they are called on.

question: The first parameter of every method, which refers to the object it was called on, is named ___.
correct: self
feedback: By convention the first parameter is self, the object the method acts on.

question: What is an attribute?
correct: A piece of data stored on an object, such as self.name
incorrect: A function defined outside of any class
A module imported from the standard library
The keyword that creates a new class
feedback: An attribute is data that belongs to an object. You set it with self.name = ... and read it back with object.name.

question: Inside a method, write the line that sets this object's attribute x to 0.
correct: self.x = 0
feedback: self.x = 0 stores 0 in the x attribute of the current object.

incorrect: None
feedback: __init__ sets n to 0, then each bump() adds 1 to this object's n. After two calls, c.n is 2.

question: What is inheritance in object-oriented programming?
correct: Building a child class on a parent so the child reuses the parent's attributes and methods
incorrect: Copying a class file into a new module before editing it
Storing several objects of the same class inside a list
Calling a method automatically when an object is created
feedback: Inheritance lets a child class build on a parent, getting the parent's attributes and methods for free and adding or changing only what is different.

question: What does  super()  refer to inside a child class?
correct: The parent class, so you can reuse its code
incorrect: The child object that was just created
The most general object in all of Python
A brand-new copy of the current class
feedback: super() gives access to the parent class. A common use is super().__init__(...) to run the parent's setup instead of retyping it.

question: What does it mean to override a method?
correct: A child class defines a method with the same name, and its version wins for child objects
incorrect: A child class hides the parent's method so neither one runs
Two methods in one class are given the exact same name
A method is renamed so it no longer conflicts with another
feedback: Overriding means the child provides its own version of a parent method. For a child object, the child's version is used instead of the parent's.

question: What is polymorphism?
correct: One method name producing different behavior depending on the object
incorrect: One object being stored under several different names
One class being split into several smaller modules
One variable changing its data type while running
feedback: Polymorphism means the same method name (like speak()) does the right thing for each kind of object, because each class can define its own version.

question: Why call  super().__init__(...)  in a child class's  __init__?
correct: To run the parent's setup code instead of retyping it
incorrect: To stop the parent class from being used again
To create a second, unrelated object in memory
To delete the attributes the parent would set
feedback: super().__init__(...) reuses the parent's initialization so the child does not have to repeat code the parent already handles.

question: What is encapsulation?
correct: Bundling data with the methods that act on it and guarding how it is changed
incorrect: Hiding a class so no other code can import it
Combining two classes into one larger class
Running a method automatically at object creation
feedback: Encapsulation keeps an object's data together with the methods that use it, and changes the data only through those methods to keep it valid.

question: What is abstraction in the context of OOP and computer science?
correct: Hiding complicated details behind a simple surface you can use
incorrect: Storing data in the smallest possible number of bits
Writing a program without using any classes at all
Translating Python source code directly into binary
feedback: Abstraction lets you use something through a simple interface without knowing its inner workings, like driving a car without understanding the engine.

question: Which of the following are the four pillars of object-oriented programming? (Select all that apply)
correct: Encapsulation
Abstraction
Inheritance
Polymorphism
incorrect: Compilation
Iteration
feedback: The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism. Compilation and iteration are real ideas but are not OOP pillars.

question: Match each pillar of object-oriented programming to its description.

pairs.definition: Bundling data with the methods that guard it
Hiding inner details behind a simple surface
A child class reusing a parent's features
One method name behaving differently per object

feedback: These four ideas define object-oriented design: bundle and guard, hide details, reuse via parents, and let one name do many things.

question: How do you implement a small abstract data type (ADT) as a class?
correct: Hide the storage inside the object and expose it only through methods
incorrect: Store all of the data in plain global variables
Let other code read and edit the storage directly
Avoid writing any methods so the data stays simple
feedback: An ADT as a class keeps its storage private and offers a set of methods (the interface). Other code uses the methods, so the storage can change without breaking it.

question: What does the noun/verb heuristic suggest when designing classes?
correct: Nouns in the problem become classes and attributes; verbs become methods
incorrect: Every noun must become a separate module file
Verbs become classes and nouns become methods
Only nouns matter, since verbs are handled by Python
feedback: As a design starter, the things in a problem (nouns) suggest classes and their data, while the actions (verbs) suggest methods.

question: A class is said to have high cohesion when it:
correct: Focuses on a single, clear responsibility
incorrect: Depends heavily on many other classes
Contains as many methods as possible
Stores its data in a shared global list
feedback: High cohesion means a class does one job well. Combined with low coupling (few dependencies), it makes code easier to change.

question: When should you prefer composition (a 'has-a' relationship) over inheritance (an 'is-a' relationship)?
correct: When one object merely contains another, rather than being a kind of it
incorrect: When the two classes share the exact same name
When you want to avoid writing any methods
When the child is a more specific kind of the parent
feedback: Use inheritance for 'is-a' (a Dog is an Animal) and composition for 'has-a' (a Car has an Engine). If one thing only contains another, compose.

question: Match each object-oriented design term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: How focused a class is on one responsibility
How dependent classes are on one another
Building an object out of other objects
Replacing a parent's method in a child class

feedback: Good design aims for high cohesion and low coupling, uses composition for 'has-a' links, and overrides methods to specialize behavior.

question: A method runs  count = count + 1  instead of  self.count = self.count + 1. What goes wrong?
correct: It updates a local variable, so the object's attribute never changes
incorrect: The program refuses to define the class at all
Every object's count is increased at the same time
The attribute count is deleted from the object
feedback: Forgetting self. creates a throwaway local variable. The update vanishes when the method ends, and the object's real attribute is untouched.

question: A class stores  items = []  directly in the class body (not inside __init__). Why is this a classic bug?
correct: Every object shares the one list, so adding to one changes them all
incorrect: Lists are not allowed to appear inside a class body
The list is deleted as soon as an object is created
Each object gets a list that can never be changed
feedback: A mutable class attribute is shared by every instance. To give each object its own list, create it inside __init__ with self.items = [].

question: Which of the following are true about the 'forgot self.' and 'shared mutable class attribute' bugs? (Select all that apply)
correct: Forgetting self. makes an update disappear when the method ends
A mutable class attribute is shared across every object
Putting self.items = [] in __init__ gives each object its own list
incorrect: Both bugs cause Python to refuse to start the program
Both bugs only appear in classes that use inheritance
feedback: Forgetting self. loses the change to a local variable; a class-body list is shared by all instances. Creating the list in __init__ fixes the sharing. Neither bug stops the program from running.
